title: The CV That Gets You Interviews
excerpt: Recruiters scan a CV in seconds, and software searches it before any human does. Here is how to rewrite your bullets, tailor every application, and build a CV that survives both filters.
content:
Ask anyone who hires in Lagos, Nairobi or Accra what happens when a graduate role goes online. Hundreds of applications land within days. A shortlist of eight or nine comes out the other side. And if you ask recruiters how they get through the pile, they'll tell you plainly: they don't read CVs. They scan them.

That one fact should change how you write yours forever. Nobody reads a CV, not at first. It gets scanned twice: once by software, once by a busy human. The CV that gets you interviews is the one built to survive both scans.

The stakes are real because the queue is long. The African Development Bank and the ILO estimate that 10 to 12 million young Africans enter the labour market every year, competing for about three million formal jobs. You can't shorten that queue. You can make sure your two pages beat the rest of it.

Scan one: the software

Most large employers run applications through an applicant tracking system, an ATS. Among America's biggest companies, 97.8 percent of the Fortune 500 use one, and the same platforms, Workday, SuccessFactors, Greenhouse, sit behind the careers pages of the banks, telcos and consultancies hiring across Africa.

Here's what an ATS actually does, because the myths are wild. It does not secretly bin your application. It parses your CV into a searchable database, and recruiters then search that database the way you search Google. In Jobscan's research, 76.4 percent of recruiters said they search and rank candidates using skills pulled straight from the job description.

Read that again. If the advert says "financial reporting" and your CV only says "prepared accounts", you may never appear in the results. You weren't rejected. You were invisible.

Two rules follow. First, mirror the exact language of the advert wherever it's honest to do so. Second, keep the file simple enough for software to parse: one column, standard headings, no text boxes, no CV designed like a poster in a graphics app.

Scan two: the human

When your CV does reach a person, you get seconds. An eye-tracking study by the careers site Ladders found that recruiters spend an average of 7.4 seconds on their first look at a CV, up from about six seconds when the study first ran in 2012.

The same study showed what wins those seconds: simple layouts, clear section headings, bold job titles and bulleted accomplishments. What loses them: dense paragraphs, multiple columns, clutter and no white space.

In that first pass, a recruiter's eyes jump to your current title and company, your previous role, and your dates, checking for progression. If those things aren't findable at a glance, the scan ends early. Bold your job titles. Keep your dates aligned. Let the page breathe.

The real divide: duty bullets vs achievement bullets

Once you survive both scans, one thing decides whether you get the call. Most CVs list duties. Interview-winning CVs list achievements.

A duty bullet describes the chair you sat in. An achievement bullet describes what changed because you were sitting in it. Watch the difference:

Before: Responsible for managing the company's social media accounts.
After: Grew Instagram followers for an Accra fashion retailer from 2,000 to 11,500 in eight months, generating about a third of all online orders.

Before: Handled customer complaints.
After: Resolved an average of 30 customer queries a day at a Nairobi telecoms call centre and held a satisfaction rating above 90 percent for six straight months.

Before: Member of the sales team.
After: Managed a route of 120 small retailers across southern Johannesburg and grew its monthly airtime revenue by 18 percent in one year.

The formula is simple: strong verb, specific task, measurable result. And no, you don't need a corner office to have numbers. Count what you already have: people trained, customers served, money handled, hours saved, events run, records digitised. If a result truly can't be measured, borrow scale instead: the size of the team, the budget you worked within, the deadline you beat.

One warning: never inflate. Interviewers love nothing more than asking you to explain a number, so every figure on your CV should come with a story you can tell for two minutes without sweating. Get that right and your CV becomes your script when you walk into the interview room prepared.

Tailoring: fifteen minutes that beat four hundred rivals

The UK's National Careers Service gives every jobseeker the same instruction: tailor your CV to the job you're applying for. Almost nobody actually does it. That's your opening.

Here's the fifteen-minute version. Read the advert twice and underline every skill or phrase that appears more than once. Pick the six or eight you honestly own. Make sure each one appears in your CV, in the advert's own words. Then reorder your bullets so the most relevant achievement sits first under each role.

Same facts, new emphasis. You're not writing fiction, you're answering the question this particular employer asked. It also pays to aim your effort where hiring is strongest, and some sectors across Africa are hiring much faster than others.

Quick teardown: weak lines and stronger rewrites

Weak lineStronger rewrite
Hardworking team player with good communication skillsTrained six new interns who went on to produce weekly market reports for 40 clients
Duties included data entry and filingDigitised 1,200 client records in three months, cutting file retrieval from a day to minutes
Assisted with eventsCoordinated logistics for a 300-person careers fair in Lagos, delivered on budget across 12 vendor contracts
Proficient in Microsoft ExcelBuilt an Excel dashboard tracking weekly sales for 15 branches, flagging stock shortages a week earlier than before

What to cut

Cut the objective statement that says you seek "a challenging role in a dynamic organisation": it says nothing. Cut "references available on request": recruiters assume it. Cut the passport photo unless the advert demands one. Cut skill bars, star ratings and decorative graphics: parsers choke on them and humans skip them. Cut any job so old or unrelated that it steals space from your best material.

And remember that the strongest CV is one a human is already expecting. A referral gets your document opened with warm eyes, which is why your network usually finds jobs before job boards do.

The final checklist

Before you hit submit, run down this list:

  • One column, clear headings, a standard font like Arial or Calibri at size 11 or bigger.
  • Two pages maximum. One page if you're a student or fresh graduate.
  • Name, city, phone, professional email and LinkedIn at the top. No full house address needed.
  • Job titles in bold, dates accurate, progression visible at a glance.
  • Every bullet starts with a verb, and at least half your bullets carry a number.
  • The advert's key skills appear in your CV in the advert's own words, honestly.
  • No objective statement, no photo unless requested, no "references available on request".
  • Saved in the format the advert asks for, with a clean file name like Ada-Obi-CV.pdf.
  • Read aloud once to catch typos, then reviewed by one person who will tell you the truth.

Your CV is not your biography. It's an advert with a single job: persuading a stranger to spend more than 7.4 seconds on you. Build it for the scan, load it with achievements, tailor it every single time, and the interview invitations will start finding you.
